title: Enduring Learning
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien draws five parallels between his experience of backyard ultramarathons and explicit teaching. Slow is smooth and smooth is fast: rushing through content leaves students unable to build on what comes next, much as running early laps too fast drained him and ended his race. Planning matters in both, with the teacher unable to control the weather of student behaviour but able to control the climate. Feedback is a direction, not a judgement, and a check for understanding tells the teacher where to go next. Practice makes permanence, as we remember what we rehearse, which is why spaced retrieval and interleaving matter. Finally, learning is a slow accumulation, like the 10 percent rule for raising running volume or couch-to-5k, so knowledge must be sequenced brick by brick. The extended metaphor is anchored in cognitive science references such as Bjork's desirable difficulties, working memory and Wiliam on feedback.
points: Moving fast through additive curriculum fails because students who miss a step cannot connect anything that follows.
Planning pace, sequencing and questioning is what separates a great lesson from one an experienced teacher can merely wing.
Feedback should work like detective work that points students back to the path, and teachers receive feedback too from student attention and checks for understanding.
Rehearsal cements both correct and incorrect responses, which supports guided practice and spaced retrieval over self-taught discovery.
The 10 percent running rule illustrates why knowledge must accumulate in carefully sequenced increments rather than all at once.
quotes: So much of what we teach in a number of different subjects is designed that the content is additive to what was learned previously. This means that if students do not understand the teaching the first time, chances are they will not understand anything that comes after that step as they cannot make meaningful connections. So although you’ll be able to move quickly for a short period, you’ll come to a grinding halt in the near future.

An experienced teacher may be able to wing a good lesson without a plan, but a great lesson is deliberate with consideration put into pace, sequencing and questioning to maximise the productive use of learning time. Our planning must also consider the bigger picture and how individual lessons fit into the wider goals of the subject.

The known unknowns can be tricky, the biggest of which being the weather. Dr Nathaniel Swain once said on the Chalk Dust podcast “students are the weather but the teacher controls the climate” and that is so true across both ideas here.

Feedback is not a judgement on overall performance, it is a direction pushing us towards what we should do next. I’ve always loved the way in which Dylan Wiliam says that feedback should be like detective work for students. It does not give them the answer but it guides them back onto the path towards the correct answer.
We remember what we rehearse and practice. This is true of both the correct and incorrect responses.

Knowledge is the same, we don’t expect students to understand the whole topic all at once. This is why we sequence learning carefully and build on top of prior learning brick by brick until we’re completed a house which could not be blown down by the mighty lungs of the Big Bad Wolf (or your local exam body).
